chapter: Decca years and the First Herd
title: Dave Tough and Don Lamond: the drummers of the Herds
summary: Herman describes Davey Tough's timekeeping and discipline, then Don Lamond, whom he gave a free hand in the Second Herd.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Prior to that, I was going to might as well talk to you a little bit about the rhythm section in that first herd.
Davey Tough. Davie Tufts.

Oh, Davie Tufts set the pattern there, I think. In fact, I'm sure he did. I remember when I hired Well, Davey Tough Davie, Chubby was still new in the band, and he said, "Is that the guy that used to be with Tommy Dorsey?" And I said, "Yeah." He said, "Do you think he'll fit the band?" I said, "Oh, yeah," I said, "Yeah, he'll fit the band."
Well, anyway, two days later, after Davey got there, Chubby had decided he invented Davey. Davey.
(Laughter.)

No, but it was really -- they didn't believe that one person so diminutive, who looked like he was about ready to cave in most days, and really would -- had absolutely no technique, and didn't want any. So -- and yet, could propel a band and just make everybody -- put everyone into a relaxed position.
How do you do that? What's your feeling about it? How was he able to do that?
Well, I think that he was just a dynamic time keeper, that there was never one ever quite like him, who took

great pride in his cymbals, the sound of each one, the heads on his drums. He was a very musical person without realizing it. He didn't read or any of that stuff, but he was a meticulous musician as far as his taste and ability.
And he kept you straight, he kept you musically straight, plus timewise you were at home, no matter where you were.
I see. So dependable.

That's right. And it taught a great deal to people, some of the younger players that -- I think it's that they were forced to take on a different discipline than they were used to. This made for a very tight, big band.
Had you been aiming to get him?
Not really, except I always knew that he played with the right guys and he knew just what to do.
I see.
And it was just one of those things. I said if we're going to have to get a drummer that will fit with what we're into, we'd better get somebody who's going to keep us together.
I see.
And that was really my basic thinking, because Davy had been through every Dixieland contingent and through every other kind of contingent. Name it, he'd been there.

And, of course, when he had to leave the band and the guys made the replacement, really, because I did not know Don Lamont at that point at all. He was the discovery of the band, and then I found another kind of drummer who had a lot of Davey's attributes but also had something else going -- technique and fly and the fact that he was into the new music, very much so. And consequently, when I started the Second Herd and he came back in the band, I gave him a free hand. I said, 'Look, Davy, the rhythm section will keep playing what they're supposedly -- should be doing. But I want you to feel free to throw frills and bombs and do whatever you want whenever you feel it.'
I see.
So he had his own little launching pad going.
Yeah, yeah. So he did express himself even --
That's right.
That's great.
Sure, and that's why I think we were able to come up with certain kinds of things.
